extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, attorneys who practice before the USPTO, and USPTO disciplinary/compliance stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: A USPTO Final Order describing stipulated facts, legal conclusions, mitigating factors, and the agreed sanctions for a registered patent attorney who submitted checks that were returned for insufficient funds. The document sets out applicable regulatory provisions, the misconduct found, remedial/mitigating considerations, and procedural steps for imposing or lifting discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional authority for discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over this matter pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.20 and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes the statutory and regulatory bases under which the Office of Enrollment and Discipline may bring and resolve disciplinary proceedings against registered practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and applicability of disciplinary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent, as an attorney registered to practice before the USPTO, is subject to the Disciplinary Rules of the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility set forth at 37 C.F.R. § 10.20 et seq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration (with a registration number) brings an attorney within the scope of USPTO professional responsibility rules; the cited regulations define proscribed conduct and disciplinary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO fee payment requirement (advance payment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees and charges payable to the USPTO are required to be paid in advance; that is, at the time of requesting any action by the USPTO for which a fee or charge is payable. See 37 C.F.R. § 1.22.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should ensure fees are paid at the time of filing/requesting actions. The regulation is a baseline expectation and is relevant to assessing misconduct when fees are not properly paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible fee payment methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent application and related fees may be paid by check, cashier's check, money order, credit card (37 C.F.R. § 1.23), electronic funds transfer from U.S. bank accounts, or by authorization to charge a USPTO deposit account (37 C.F.R. § 1.25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists acceptable payment mechanisms and implies practitioner responsibility to use reliable payment methods and ensure sufficient funds or established deposit accounts when using them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for filing date assignment without basic filing fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. § 1.53, applications for patent may be assigned a filing date without payment of the basic filing fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrow regulatory exception does not negate the general requirement that fees be paid in advance for other actions; practitioners should be aware of limited exceptions but not rely on them broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct defined: issuing checks drawn on insufficient funds
rubrics_metrics.description: By signing and submitting checks to the Office drawn on insufficient funds that were subsequently returned when the USPTO presented the checks for payment, Respondent violated Disciplinary Rules 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(b)(5) (proscribing conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice) and 10.23(b)(6) (proscribing engaging in conduct reflecting adversely on a practitioner's fitness to practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuing checks that bounce for payment of required USPTO fees is identified as conduct that can be prejudicial to administration of justice and adversely reflect on fitness to practice; such acts are a basis for disciplinary sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner bookkeeping and fiduciary responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent admits that he did not always keep adequate track of the funds deposited into and disbursed from his law firm's checking account, which led to issuing checks that were returned for insufficient funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate bookkeeping and account oversight are expected; failures that lead to bounced checks or unpaid USPTO fees are actionable and relevant to discipline. Remedial training (e.g., trust account school) is recognized as responsive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial actions as mitigating conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedial action taken prior to notice of investigation—such as using online banking for real-time balances, using credit/debit cards instead of checks, maintaining a deposit account, making good on returned checks, paying returned-check processing fees, informing clients, and completing a Client Trust Account School—are presented as mitigating measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented, proactive remedial steps that correct the underlying cause and reduce risk of recurrence are considered in mitigation when imposing discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors considered in discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant mitigating factors include being a registered practitioner for over 20 years without prior disciplinary history and unequivocal acceptance of responsibility for bookkeeping errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length of clean practice and acceptance of responsibility weigh in favor of reduced discipline; these factors are explicitly reflected in the agreed-upon sanction (stayed suspension and probation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreed sanction structure: stayed suspension and probation
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is suspended for 24 months from practice before the USPTO, with the suspension immediately stayed and the stay to remain in effect while Respondent serves a 24-month probationary period; Respondent is permitted to practice during probation unless the stay is lifted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office may impose a suspension but stay its operation conditioned on probationary compliance; this allows continued practice subject to future review and potential activation of suspension for noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order to Show Cause and response timeline for probation violations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the OED Director believes Respondent failed to comply during probation, the OED Director shall issue an Order to Show Cause, send it to Respondent's address of record, and grant Respondent fifteen (15) days to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the procedural steps and minimal notice/response window the OED follows before recommending lifting the stay of suspension; ensures an opportunity to respond prior to further action.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Director recommendation and lifting of stay process
rubrics_metrics.description: If after consideration of Respondent's response the OED Director remains of the opinion that Respondent failed to comply, the OED Director shall deliver the Order to Show Cause, Respondent's response, and argument/evidence to the USPTO Director and request that the stay be lifted and Respondent suspended for up to 24 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains escalation from OED to USPTO Director and the evidentiary/argument materials the OED forwards when recommending lifting a stayed suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences if suspension is activated
rubrics_metrics.description: If Respondent is suspended pursuant to the provisions, (1) Respondent shall comply with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; (2) the OED Director shall disseminate information in accordance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.59; (3) USPTO shall promptly dissociate Respondent's name from all USPTO customer numbers and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) certificates; (4) Respondent shall not use any USPTO customer number or PKI certificate unless and until he is reinstated; and (5) Respondent may not obtain a USPTO customer number or PKI certificate unless and until he is reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies immediate operational and public-notice consequences that follow an imposed suspension, including dissociation from customer credentials and the mechanics of public dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice of discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall publish this Final Order at the Office of Enrollment and Discipline's Reading Room electronically and give notice of the public discipline and the reasons for the discipline to disciplinary enforcement agencies in the states where the Respondent is admitted, to courts where Respondent is known to be admitted, and to the public in accordance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.59; the OED will also publish a Notice of Stayed Suspension in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public posting and interjurisdictional notice are routine parts of disciplinary outcomes and serve both transparency and notice to other enforcement authorities and courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disciplinary record in future proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the agreement prevents the Office from considering the record of this disciplinary proceeding, including this Final Order, when addressing any further complaint or evidence of similar misconduct and/or in any future disciplinary proceeding as an aggravating factor or to rebut statements by or on Respondent's behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior disciplinary record may be used against a practitioner later; settlement does not preclude future reliance on the record in aggravation or rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restitution and administrative fees as remedial requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent made good on the returned checks and paid the returned check processing fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where misconduct causes financial impact (e.g., returned checks), restitution and payment of administrative fees are expected remedial acts and are relevant to mitigation and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of costs between parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director and Respondent shall each bear their own costs incurred to date and in carrying out the terms of this agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement can include mutual bearing of costs rather than shifting fees; this is a possible disposition term in disciplinary agreements.
